Οἱ μὲν γὰρ οὐκ εἰσάπαν ἀπονενεύκασιν ἐπὶ τὸ χρῆναι πλημμελεῖν, ἀλλ' ἴσασι μὲν, ἀῤῥωστοῦντες ἔσθ' ὅτε, καὶ ταῖς τῆς σαρκὸς ἐνεχόμενοι πλεονεξίαις, καὶ οὐκ ἀφεστάναι τῶν ἄλλων αἰτιαμάτων βούλονται. «Πολλὰ γὰρ πταίομεν ἅπαντες,» κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον. Ἀποσείονται δ' οὖν ὅμως ὡς ἀκαλλὲς τὸ γυμνῶς ἐθέλειν ἀσχημονεῖ
pass_a_gloss: §22 dual gloss: λεπίς / scales · πτερύγιον / fins · ἀλαζονεία / arrogance … Pass A ≠ Pass B. Theme: Scales cover shame; fins raise mind; uncovered vice.
pass_b_english: Cyril: ...let us live, we will do this or that, and now you boast in your arrogances.' So then as fishes we swim-through this broad and spacious sea, that is, the world; for somehow different is each one's life. For some have not altogether bent-away unto the needing to fault, but they know on the one hand, being weak sometimes, and being held by the greedinesses of the flesh, and they do not wish to stand-off from the other charges. 'For many things we all stumble,' according to the having-been-written. Yet they shake-off somehow as unbeautiful the wishing nakedly to be shameful. And no one would persuade to practice the faulting manifest and unshadowed. And they care very much for the needing to escape-notice. 'For wise ones will hide their own shames,' according to the having-been-written. This, I think, is the as in an order of a covering to have the scales. And they swim-up very often also unto the on-high, for they look, not unto the below through all, and they think also the above, and they flee-through easily those who would somehow choose to net unto destruction; this someone will say the as it were to have used fins intelligibly, and to make very hot the movement of the mind.
Palladius: Fitting things you spoke; for somehow the riddle carries-away toward thinking the word to hold thus.

Cyril: And some fault, not having drawn-under, but practicing as it were naked and altogether uncovered the worthlessness; and about them one would say well: 'Whose glory is in their shame.' For they have always bent toward uncleanness, and rolling-in the lowest muds, they are beasts according to the true, or some other beside this. And such would be altogether and wholly both strengthless and easy-to-catch, being tyrannized by the pleasures unto every whatever of the outlandish. Or is not somehow such the life of the having-been-despaired?
